summary: In Greek mythology, the Ourea were the primordial deities who personified the mountains. They were among the first beings born of Gaia (Earth) by parthenogenesis, produced alongside Uranus (the Sky) and Pontus (the Sea) and thus belonging to the oldest stratum of the cosmos. Rather than a set of individually named gods, the Ourea functioned as a collective embodiment of the hills and mountain ranges themselves, conceived as the dwelling-places of the mountain Nymphs. No organized cult of the Ourea is attested in the surviving ancient sources.
etymology: The name comes from Ancient Greek oûros (singular), "mountain, hill," with the plural form oúrea (Οὔρεα) translating simply as "mountains."

sections.heading: Origin
paragraphs: The Ourea were the parthenogenetic offspring of Gaia (Earth), produced by her without a father at the same stage of the cosmogony that brought forth Uranus (Sky) and Pontus (Sea). This places them among the primordial deities, the foundational generation of the Greek cosmos.
Hesiod records their birth in the Theogony, describing how Gaia "brought forth long hills, graceful haunts of the goddess Nymphs who dwell amongst the glens of the hills."

sections.heading: Nature and Function
paragraphs: Unlike many later figures associated with specific peaks, the Ourea were treated as a collective personification of mountains and hills rather than a roster of named individual gods. They embodied the physical landscape itself as a divine force.

Their primary association in myth is as the habitats of the mountain Nymphs, who were said to dwell in the glens and valleys of the hills. In this sense the Ourea belong to the same primordial family as Uranus, Pontus, and Gaia, filling out the early picture of the world's body alongside sky and sea.
